The medal that changed MMA's India story

New Delhi, Sep 24 (ANI): Indian athlete Suchika Tariyal, winner of the Bronze Medal in Mixed Martial Arts (MMA) at the Asian Games 2026, interacts with media as she receives a warm welcome from her family and supporters on her arrival at the airport, in New Delhi on Thursday. (ANI Photo/Neeraj)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: By the time Varun Sanyal finally reached his room in Nagoya, nearly 12 hours had passed since landing in Japan. He had flown from London to Mumbai, collected his Asian Games accreditation card, travelled via Singapore, spent hours proving he was a registered athlete, and then found himself sharing a room that wasn't meant for three people.A few days later, he was lying outside a sauna, hyperventilating after collapsing during a weight cut attempt that ended his Asian Games campaign before it had begun.Yet Sanyal, who has now returned to London, would rather remember the Asian Games as the moment mixed martial arts (MMA) forced itself into India's sporting conversation."Instead of focusing on what didn't happen, you focus on what did," he said in a conversation with TimesofIndia.com, referring to teammate Suchika Tariyal's historic bronze medal — India's first Asian Games medal in MMA.For a sport making its Asian Games debut, that perspective may prove more significant than his own heartbreak.Sanyal's road to the Games was anything but straightforward.The 26-year-old had earned qualification months earlier, but uncertainty over selection meant he shifted his attention back to his professional MMA career. Ranked among Asia's top six, he was eventually drafted into the Indian squad only two weeks before the Games after another athlete became ineligible under the Sports Ministry's selection criteria.Those two weeks became a race against time.He was recovering from a staph infection, reorganising an international training camp in England, arranging travel documents, and attempting to shed nearly five kilograms to make the lightweight limit — all while preparing for what should have been the biggest tournament of his career.On paper, Sanyal arrived in Nagoya as one of India's brightest MMA prospects. The Delhi-based fighter had already built an impressive résumé across amateur, semi-professional and professional circuits, compiling 17 bouts in just four years and establishing himself as one of the country's most active competitors. But nothing in that experience prepared him for the chaos that awaited off the cage.The accommodation chaos became one of the defining stories of Aichi-Nagoya 2026, and Sanyal finds a mention in that storyline.His name was missing from the registration list upon arrival. Officials at the Expo Hall directed him to the cruise ship that served as the Athletes' Village, where another round of explanations began from scratch. Questions over whether he was even registered followed, despite the accreditation card that had allowed him into Japan. The issue was eventually resolved only after intervention from the Indian Olympic Association (IOA), but not before an entire day had disappeared.The logistical mess exposed a deeper problem for Indian MMA.Unlike many established sports, the MMA contingent travelled without coaches being granted accreditation inside the cruise. Some of the coaches paid for their own flights, hotels and transport, while the athletes were left to manage themselves inside the village.That meant Sanyal wasn't simply preparing to compete. He became translator, manager and teammate rolled into one.He helped Suchika navigate anti-doping procedures, searched the sprawling cruise ship for medical assistance and even sprinted between decks looking for an iron to prepare India's competition kits.In another sport, those responsibilities would belong to support staff. In India's newest Games discipline, they fell to the athletes themselves.If the accommodation saga tested Sanyal's patience, the weight cut attempt tested his body.Competing in the 77kg category is slightly misleading. Because athletes weigh in wearing a gi and belt weighing around 1.5kg, competitors effectively need to reach roughly 75.5kg. Sanyal normally walks around at 80kg and had managed to cut down to 77.5kg before the final cut.Two kilograms remained and the clock was ticking down.Inside the sauna, the first few minutes were almost routine. Fighters from Kyrgyzstan, Singapore and Brunei chatted casually while everyone sweated through the final stages of preparation. Then dehydration began taking over.Sanyal remembers measuring time only through the sauna clock — one checkpoint after another. Around the 30-minute mark, he stood up, experienced a severe head rush and stumbled onto a nearby bench before collapsing."I just remember that I finally hit the 30-minute mark and I stood up. And when you're dehydrated, you start seeing black, like you're starry-eyed. You get that head rush. I was completely out of it. I push the door to the sauna, and then there's this tiny bench, which I just flat out start lying down on, and I'm hyperventilating. Honestly, this whole thing feels like a fever dream," he said with a laugh.A Nepali athlete alerted his coach, who then attempted to communicate with Japanese medical staff through a translation app while Sanyal insisted, somewhat irrationally, that he did not want water because he still needed to make weight."My body was really overheated at this point. I felt like I had a fever. I said I need to speak to my coach. Fortunately, the person near me was Nepali, so my coach spoke to him in Hindi. They then took me to a medical facility. There, my coach asked them to give me electrolytes. They spoke in Japanese and with limited English. Meanwhile, I am out of it and still saying not to give me anything because I am trying to cut weight."Eventually, doctors treated him for dehydration and overheating, and medical advice to rehydrate immediately meant his Asian Games campaign officially ended.Looking back, Sanyal thinks it wasn't the smartest decision to cut weight. Doing it alone, after frantic travel and with virtually no recovery time, only added to the risk."I have cut weight before and made it to the tournaments, so that wasn't the challenge. I think it was the short time window accompanied with all the stress, travel, etc. Plus just not having anyone there. I think had I done it in a more systematic way while I was there in the sauna, maybe."I don't want to speculate because then I start thinking of what could have been. And then it becomes a bit frustrating," he explained.While Sanyal recovered, Suchika Taiyal won a bronze medal and became the first Indian MMA athlete to stand on an Asian Games podium. Sanyal had been in her corner throughout the competition — not officially as a coach, but as the closest thing India had inside the village.Her medal, coming controversially, altered the conversation.For years, MMA in India has largely existed outside the mainstream sporting ecosystem, thriving in independent promotions while fighting for institutional recognition. The Asian Games offered legitimacy, and the medal offered proof that the country could compete with Asia's best.Sanyal believes that is the real legacy of Nagoya.The federation (MMA-SFI) itself is barely over a year old, yet India has already produced medals at the Asian Youth Games and now the senior Asian Games. For a discipline only just entering the multi-sport landscape, those results matter as much as infrastructure.His own story, strangely enough, helped too.The accomodation controversy, the viral videos that went with it, the failed attempt at playing the continental showpiece brought unprecedented attention to a sport that rarely finds itself on front pages. It wasn't the publicity he wanted, but perhaps it was the publicity Indian MMA needed."We still came away with a medal despite everything going on, which I think is huge. Two things to this. The medal showing that we (can) produce results. The federation that sent us has only been in existence for just a little over a year or so. And even at the Asian Youth Games, medals were produced. So I'd say the biggest takeaway is that the federation and the athletes have shown that MMA fighters can produce results. Now I would like the government, the corporate sponsors and the audience to get behind the MMA fighters," said Sanyal."If you ask my personal takeaway, I'm glad that there was so much interest shown. It was at my expense but the fact of the matter is so much media attention went on the sport, put on the athletes and for that I'm grateful. So for me that that's the biggest takeaway," he continued.Sanyal left Nagoya without stepping into the cage. Yet in many ways, his toughest fight had already been won: convincing an entire country that MMA belongs on its biggest sporting stage.
Article Summary: Varun Sanyal was one of India's brightest MMA prospects. Ranked among Asia's top six, he was drafted into the Indian squad only two weeks before the Games. The 26-year-old had earned qualification months earlier, but uncertainty over selection meant he shifted his attention back to his professional MMA career.

Article Title: Asian Games: Priya, Lovlina storm into semifinals as India’s boxers continue to assure medals in Aichi-Nagoya
Article Text:
Priya Ghanghas and Lovlina Borgohain

Lovlina assures second successive Asiad medal

Priya joins growing list of Indian semifinalists

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India’s boxing campaign continued to gather momentum at the Asian Games 2026 as Priya Ghanghas and Lovlina Borgohain powered into the semifinals on Monday, assuring the country of two more medals in the ring. The duo’s victories added to an already growing list of Indian boxers who have reached the last four, underlining the sport’s contribution to India’s medal haul in Aichi-Nagoya.Lovlina, the Tokyo Olympics bronze medallist, produced a commanding 5-0 unanimous-decision victory over South Korea’s Seong Suyeon in the women’s 75kg quarterfinal. The win guaranteed the Assam boxer at least a bronze medal and a second successive Asian Games podium finish after her silver at Hangzhou in 2023.Priya followed with another 5-0 victory, overcoming Tajikistan’s Mijgona Samadova in the women’s 60kg quarterfinal to book her place in the last four.Competing in her first bout of the tournament, Lovlina made an aggressive start against Seong, repeatedly using her jab-cross combination to unsettle the South Korean. Although Seong attempted to use her height advantage and landed a barrage of punches in the second round, Lovlina’s movement and cleaner combinations kept her in control.The Indian continued to find openings with her crosses and hooks before finishing strongly with quick 1-2 combinations. The judges awarded her all three rounds, giving her a comprehensive 5-0 victory.For Lovlina, the medal continues an impressive run across major international competitions. She won silver at the previous Asian Games and also claimed Commonwealth Games silver last month, adding to medals won at the World Championships, Asian Championships and World Cup.Lovlina will face Kazakhstan’s reigning 70kg world champion Natalya Bogdanova in the semifinal.Priya, the Asian Championship gold medallist and reigning Commonwealth Games champion, also secured her place on the podium with a unanimous decision against Samadova.Her progress means India now have multiple boxers assured of medals, with Parveen Hooda (65kg), Ankush Panghal (80kg) and Narender Berwal (+90kg) having already entered the semifinals on Sunday.Parveen defeated Uzbekistan’s World Championships silver medallist Navbakhor Khamidova 5-0, while Ankush recorded a similar unanimous-decision win over Tajikistan’s Nekruz Salimov. Narender also advanced to the last four in the +90kg category.India had returned from the previous Asian Games with four boxing medals, including one silver and three bronze. With the competition still having several rounds to go in Aichi-Nagoya, the Indian boxing contingent has already positioned itself for another significant contribution to the country’s medal tally.Kapil Pokhariya is also in action on Monday in the men’s 90kg quarterfinal, giving India another opportunity to add to its growing list of semifinalists.
Article Summary: Priya Ghanghas and Lovlina Borgohain reach semifinals of Asian Games 2026. Priya beats Tajikistan’s Mijgona Samadova 5-0 to book her place in the last four. The win guaranteed the Assam boxer at least a bronze medal and a second successive Asian Games podium finish after her silver at Hangzhou in 2023. The victory added to an already growing list of Indian boxers who have reached the lastFour.

Article Title: At 15, Joshna Chinappa made her Asian Games debut; 24 years later, she has seven appearances and six medals
Article Text:
Joshna Chinappa and Velavan Senthilkumar show their bronze medal (ANI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NAGOYA: When Joshna Chinappa became the British Junior Open U-17 champion in 2003, her current teammates Anahat Singh and Shameena Riaz were not even born.Inside the glass walls of the squash court, Joshna did more than redefine how the game could be played by Indian women. Alongside Dipika Pallikal, the other women pioneer of the sport in India, she helped rewrite the narrative for women in squash.On Saturday, at the Nagoya Kinjo Futo Arena, in her record seven Asian Games appearances, Joshna added her sixth medal, a bronze. The medal came after a contentious decision denied her and Velavan Senthilkumar a place in the mixed doubles final.Senthilkumar and Joshna then went into the mixed doubles final. It was a call the 40-year-old found difficult to stomach, but one she knows she will eventually have to move past.“I’ll have to get over it. That’s life, right? As an athlete, it’s important to be able to bounce back from those decisions and tough matches. My career is filled with that. So, as much as I am disappointed, and it’ll take me a couple of days, I’ll be back,” Joshna reflected, during a chat with TOI.Joshna’s Asian Games journey began as a teenager, and the memories of that first appearance remain vivid.“I was barely 15 when I went for my first Asian Games (Busan 2002). That memory is still clear because I was young and was meeting all the superstars of Indian sport for the first time. They were so much older, it was very intimidating.“But I also learned so much. I knew I’d still be playing from back then,” she said.Staying at the top of a gruelling sport for so long has meant embracing the daily grind. Joshna trains for five to six hours a day, driven by the belief that representing India is about more than simply being part of the squad.“It’s such a privilege and great responsibility to be able to play for India and to be a person who can still contribute to the medals. I never wanted to be someone who just made up numbers in the team. The girls are so much younger and are doing really well, so it’s important that I contribute as well,” she said.Her commitment even extended to a small personal sacrifice. Three months ago, she gave up chocolates to keep her sweet tooth in check until the Games.There will, however, be no attempt at one final Olympic chapter. Joshna has ruled out a shot at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, where squash will make its debut.
Article Summary: Joshna Chinappa won a bronze medal at the Asian Games in Nagoya. The 40-year-old was denied a place in the mixed doubles final. Joshna has ruled out a shot at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, where squash will make its debut.

Article Title: Asian Games 2026: Abhay, Anahat’s upset bids fall short as Malaysia retain squash singles titles
Article Text:
India's Anahat Singh (ANI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NAGOYA: For Abhay Singh and Anahat Singh, the singles squash finals were always going to be a tough ask. But they lent hope after their stirring semifinal victories, that the Indian duo could produce another upset and punch their tickets to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.Instead, both had to settle for silver, losing to Malaysia’s defending champions, who used their greater experience, tactical nous and game awareness to tilt the finals in their favour. Abhay went down 9-11, 5-11, 5-11 to nemesis Yow Eain Yow in 44 minutes, while Anahat was beaten 4-11, 4-11, 7-11 by Sivasangari Subramaniam.For Anahat, the women’s final was less about how she lost and more about how comprehensively Sivasangari controlled the contest. The Indian teenager made a bright start, going toe-to-toe with the Malaysian and opening up a 3-2 lead. But her drop shots soon began to unravel, offering Sivasangari the opening she needed. The defending champion seized it and never allowed Anahat back into the game.The Indian struggled to match Sivasangari’s pace and movement, while the Malaysian repeatedly found ways through her defence. The second game followed much the same script, with Anahat searching for answers to her opponent’s attacking game.After the dramatic comeback against Japan’s Satomi Watanabe in the semifinal, there was hope Anahat could produce another fightback. Sivasangari, however, gave her no room to launch one, closing out the match and securing the Olympic berth.For Anahat, the defeat was another lesson in a week that offered plenty of them. “The past week has been a learning experience in terms of how to handle pressure and play against more experienced players. I’m going to rewatch all the matches and try to learn as much as I can from it,” she said. The 18-year-old admitted she was disappointed with her performance. “I’m not happy with the way I played. I could have done a lot better. Maybe I got a bit too happy after the semifinal win and the adrenaline was too high,” she said.Abhay, meanwhile, came up against an opponent he has never beaten. The Indian kept the opening game tight, engaging Yow in long rallies. But a missed shot gave the Malaysian an opening, which he duly exploited. There were prolonged exchanges of backhand drop shots, but they eventually began to take their toll on Abhay’s legs and his movement slowed down. Once Yow edged the opening game, he took control, retrieving almost everything Abhay threw at him and repeatedly blunting the Indian’s attacks.“I’m disappointed with the result. To be honest, I have nothing to celebrate because I didn’t come here to win the silver. That said, sometimes you need to put your hands up and give credit to your opponent. I think he deserved to win,” Abhay conceded.
Article Summary: Abhay Singh and Anahat Singh both lose in singles squash finals. Abhay beaten by nemesis Yow Eain Yow in 44 minutes. Anah at beaten by Sivasangari Subramaniam in 4-11, 4- 11, 7-11.

Article Title: Trend, research, repeat: How Gen Z is shopping for the festive season
Article Text:
Young shoppers are taking a more considered approach to festive purchases (AI Image)

Social media not only sets trends but allows shoppers to find out what the latest festive season fashion is looking like

‘Upcycling remains a favourite’

Last year, we took a festive shopping trip to Janpath’s Gujarati Market, where Times Fresh Face contestants Divyanshi Sachi and Bhavini Rana joined us to explore Navratri looks

Tracking trends, hunting deals

I mostly come across festive fashion trends via Instagram and then do a deep dive research about them on Pinterest to see whether I like them enough to buy them Kanishka Mukhija, 20, student and makeup artist

‘Instagram and Pinterest are major sources of reference’

For Gen Z, festive shopping is no longer just about spotting a trend and grabbing it at the local market or adding it to your cart (AI Image)

From

Lajpat Nagar

to online carts





For Gen Z, festive shopping is no longer just about spotting a trend and grabbing it at the local market or adding it to your cart. From discovering looks on Instagram and Pinterest to checking Reddit reviews, comparing prices and giving old outfits a new spin, young shoppers are taking a more considered approach to festive purchases. A recent study by Snapchat-GWI found that seven in 10 Gen Z consumers said creator content helps them discover products, while four in 10 actively seek opinions or advice before making a purchase.You may call Gen Z unserious, but they don’t kid when it comes to shopping. “My favourite hack has to be upcycling mom’s saris and suits. Last year for Diwali, I turned my mom’s silk saree into a coord set, and it turned out great. That’s one hack I like to follow. I also use my mom’s and nani’s jewellery that I can style in my own way. I like to use trending prints as borders on simple outfits to make them shine for the festive season. Gota patti was trending recently, and I used a flashy gota patti lace and asked my tailor to stitch it on my plain kurta. It turned into a completely new outfit,” shares Aanvi, 21, a working professional.Karnika Chandana, 27, adds that while following trends is fun, she prefers a blend of traditional outfits and trendy looks, “I don’t want my festive outfits to feel too trend-driven because traditional silhouettes have a timeless charm.But I do like adding a modern touch through the blouse, draping, jewellery, colours or styling. For me, the outfit should still feel festive and Indian but not look dated.”For some, online shopping is an easier way to get the best deals and keep an eye out for trends. Dippra Pathak, 25, a working professional, notes, “With online shopping, I can check out the same outfits from multiple places at different prices. I can see the reviews and check the quality, and whether it looks the same for other shoppers. I usually prefer Reddit for reviews because they’re very honest.” She adds that, to avoid missing out on sales, she keeps her cart and wishlist updated and checks them regularly to keep track of price drops.Young shoppers have also incorporated AI to compare prices, find trends and look for the best deals online. Prompts to analyse and differentiate between bot and real reviews have been popular online. “I have used AI occasionally when I’m trying to compare options or find out what’s trending. But I usually use it as a starting point rather than relying on it. I still check Instagram, ecommerce websites and customer reviews before buying something,” Karnika says.Social media not only sets trends but allows shoppers to find out what the latest festive season fashion is looking like. Kanishka Mukhija, 20, student and makeup artist, says, “Social media has impacted all the possible aspects around festivals, in my opinion. I tend to go for make-up products to even accessories being suggested in reels and trends much more than any other suggestion. I mostly come across festive fashion trends via Instagram and then do a deep dive research about them on Pinterest to see whether I like them enough to buy them. ”Aanvi adds, “Influencers start posting like a month before the festive season. You get an idea of what the trends are going to be this season. Also, what a celeb is wearing to an event. So that becomes a trend and then eventually everybody starts replicating it. Instagram and Pinterest are major sources of reference.”Putting her own spin on luxury trends, Aanvi compares designer pieces with dupes, DIY options and online prices to get the best deal. “Personally, if I like a high-end design, I first check how much the designer is selling it for and then look for a dupe online. If I find it significantly cheaper online, I’ll buy it there. If the price is similar to getting it stitched, I’d rather get it hand-stitched by a designer and go the outfit from scratch route,” she explains, adding that Lajpat Nagar is her go-to for its wide variety of traditional and modern clothing options.Kanishka uses a mix of options. “My go-to shopping hacks include local market scouting, where I go to places like Sarojini Nagar, Lajpat Nagar and Chandni Chowk in the first half of the day to avoid crowds and find good deals, along with constantly looking out for pre-festive deals on e-commerce platforms, etc. I browse markets before buying because it definitely comes in handy for cost-effectiveness as well as in terms of variety to choose from. ”
Article Summary: Social media not only sets trends but allows shoppers to find out what the latest festive season fashion is looking like. A recent study by Snapchat-GWI found that seven in 10 Gen Z consumers said creator content helps them discover products. Four in 10 actively seek opinions or advice before making a purchase.

Article Title: Why some men commit sexual crimes? No easy answers to this
Article Text:
Image Used For Representational Purpose Only





NEW DELHI: The Astha Kunj gangrape case has again raised a difficult question: what makes some men cross the line to choose sexual assault? Psychiatrists and psychologists say the answer is not simple, and single explanation can explain all cases.Behind sexual assaults lies a complex mix of narcissistic entitlement, deviant thinking, impulsive behaviour, poor control over anger, a belief that they can escape the law and, in some cases, mental illness.None of this can or should absolve any attacker, the psychiatrists pointed out.Dr Rajiv Mehta, a psychiatrist at Sir Ganga Ram Hospital, said sexual assaulters have personality deviations and believe they can escape the law. “They can be impulsive, impatient and have a low tolerance level. They may not think through the consequences before acting. They may have a false notion that they are above the law. They can be furious and quick to act. At times, they may also be under the influence of drugs,” he said.Mehta added that some assaulters may suffer from mental illnesses, such some kind of mania or even schizophrenia. “Mania can lead to increased libido, risk-taking behaviour and other symptoms.In this particular case, the accused was disturbing others and allegedly carrying a firearm illegally,” he said.He added that society needs to be educated about mental illness and the stigma surrounding it needs to be addressed. “Behaviours have biological moorings and can be treated through medicines and counselling,” he said.Dr Rajat Mitra, a professor of forensic psychology who has worked with survivors of sexual assault for over two decades, said research had shown that sexual assaulters do not necessarily suffer from mental illness. “However, they may have deviant thinking and ideation, and relationships are complex for them. In a normal relationship, intimacy develops gradually, after affection. But this does not happen for assaulters and they perceive the use of force against a woman as natural. Sexual assault also cannot be put into one category as each case varies,” he said.Mitra added that about one-third of sexual assaults involve violent attacks as some assaulters find violence to be sexually arousing. “Several assaulters have said they could not continue with the act because they could not avoid the face or the look of the victim. To erase the sense of innocence in the victim and keep themselves going, they indulge in violent acts,” he said.Mitra said the word “rape” is derived from the Latin word raptus, meaning to seize another man’s property. Given the term’s historical and derogatory connotations, he said such incidents should be referred to as sexual assault.Dr Nimesh G Desai, a senior psychiatrist and former director of Institute of Human Behaviour and Allied Sciences (IHBAS), said: “Rapid urbanisation, rural-to-urban migration, sexual frustration, lack of fear of the law, and the influence of social media, added to innate urges, are factors that may drive a few men towards crime. However, none of these reasons is justified.”He added that the basic instinct of sexual urge has to be channelled in more ethically appropriate ways. “All men should be taught about this. All potential victims should be taught all forms of protection. A swift and equitable criminal justice system plays a very crucial role in prevention,” he said.Pulkit Sharma, a clinical psychologist and psychoanalytic therapist, said narcissistic entitlement can drive some men towards sexual assault. “In Indian society, some men hold patriarchal beliefs that they are superior to others. In recent times, certain movies and social media reels have contributed to a return of the ‘primitive man’. A few years ago, such characters were portrayed as villains, but they are now celebrated in films and on social media. ”He added that "some Indian men are unable to accept an independent woman socialising with her male friends. They may believe that they are entitled to have the same woman as well.”Sharma added that for some assaulters, the law does not act as a not a deterrent because they believe that their connections or money can help them get away.
Article Summary: The Astha Kunj gangrape case has again raised a difficult question: what makes some men cross the line to choose sexual assault? Psychiatrists and psychologists say the answer is not simple, and no single explanation can explain all cases. Behind sexual assaults lies a complex mix of narcissistic entitlement, deviant thinking, impulsive behaviour, poor control over anger and a belief that they can escape the law.

Article Title: Meet Shereen Pavlides, the former Glen Mills resident who turned home cooking into a digital career; the 1990 high school graduate now has about 5 million TikTok followers, 2 million on Facebook and 1
Article Text:
​Shereen Pavlides develops her own recipes and produces her cooking content. (Daily Times photo)

The TikTok video that changed everything

Building a career around cooking

Her advice to content creators

Shereen Pavlides did not plan to become a social media star. The Garnet Valley High School Class of 1990 graduate and former Glen Mills resident built her career around food over several years, moving from restaurant work and private mortgage insurance to culinary school, food writing and television. Today, millions of people follow her cooking content online.Pavlides is known online as Cooking With Shereen. She has built a following of about 5 million on TikTok, more than 2 million on Facebook, over 1 million on Instagram and roughly 1.45 million YouTube subscribers. Her online audience grew as she shared simple recipes and cooking techniques from her own kitchen.According to Delco Today, Pavlides' journey into food began early. As a teenager, Pavlides worked in restaurants. She later spent years in private mortgage insurance before enrolling in culinary school in New York City. That decision changed the direction of her career and led her into several food-related roles.After culinary school, Pavlides worked in food styling, food writing and recipe development. She also worked in test kitchens, including at Good Housekeeping. Her experience eventually took her to QVC, where she became an on-air guest and appeared in more than 186 live broadcasts demonstrating cookware, bakeware and kitchen appliances.Her television work played an important role in what came next. Viewers regularly asked Pavlides for her recipes, and those requests encouraged her to create content of her own.She launched her YouTube channel in 2019 and began experimenting with TikTok soon after. One of the videos that helped her gain attention was her fifth TikTok video. It was simple tutorial on making chicken cutlets. The video received millions of views and helped establish her he simple, from-scratch cooking style that became synonymous to Pavlides' online content.Pavlides continued developing recipes and filming them in her own kitchen. She also remains involved in editing her videos even as her audience grew.Her work now takes an estimated 60 to 80 hours a week. Even with a large online following, she continues to develop her own recipes and remain involved in the production of her content.The social media career has also taken Pavlides beyond online platforms. She has appeared on major television programmes and published two bestselling cookbooks. She is currently working on a third cookbook. At the same time, Pavlides is planning to expand her production team as her work continues to grow.Her career has moved from working in restaurants and food-related jobs to creating content that reaches millions of people through several platforms. However, the path has not been limited to one type of food media. Her experience in food styling, writing, recipe development, test kitchens and live television has all become part of the career she has built around her online presence.Pavlides has also shared advice for people who want to build their own careers in content creation. Speaking to aspiring creators at a recent Broadcast Pioneers event, she said creators should focus on providing something useful to their audiences.“Don’t make it about yourself. Give something that can help somebody else and be useful in their lives. Quality of your content really matters, because you are building trust,” Pavlides said.She also stresses on the importance of having a direct relationship with an audience and being genuine in the way content is presented.“Talk to your audience, not at them, and be your authentic self,” she said. “Be good at what you’re communicating and let the rest ride,” Pavlides added.What began with a YouTube channel in 2019 and early experiments on TikTok has since become Cooking With Shereen, with a large audience spread across TikTok, Facebook, Instagram and YouTube.
Article Summary: Shereen Pavlides is known online as Cooking With Shereen. She has built a following of about 5 million on TikTok, more than 2 million on Facebook, over 1 million on Instagram and roughly 1.45 million YouTube subscribers. Her online audience grew as she shared simple recipes and cooking techniques from her own kitchen.

Article Title: Post-festival cleanup effort: Students unite for beach clean-up: 207 kg of waste removed after Ganesh Visarjan
Article Text:
In the wake of the Ganesh Visarjan festivities, students and volunteers united early Sunday to clean Juhu Beach, collecting an impressive 207 kilograms of waste primarily linked to the immersions. This initiative not only underscored the importance of environmental stewardship post-celebration but also showcased collaboration with local NGOs. Participants described the experience as transformative, reminding them of the city's environmental needs amid festivities like Ganesh Visarjan.





On Sunday morning, Juhu Beach, Koliwada, Santacruz looked very different from the festive shoreline it had been just a night earlier. The sounds of celebration had faded, the crowds had dispersed and the sea had carried away countless idols offered during Ganesh Visarjan. What remained on the shore was the aftermath — flowers, plastic bags, immersion material and remnants of Ganesh idols scattered across the sand.THE MORNING AFTER BAPPA’S FAREWELLAt daybreak, 36 student volunteers arrived not to celebrate, but to clean up. Over the course of the beach clean-up drive, they collected 207 kilograms of waste, much of it linked to the previous day's immersions. The waste was segregated on-site and handed over for appropriate disposal, with the initiative focusing on reducing the impact of post-festival debris on Mumbai's coastline and mangrove ecosystem.FROM CELEBRATION TO RESPONSIBILITYThe clean-up was jointly conducted by students from a city college in association with local NGOs, with faculty, staff and student volunteers coming together early on a Sunday morning to tackle the debris left behind after the festivities. The initiative was spearheaded by Vidur Dhabaria, a city college faculty member who teaches Environmental Studies (EVS) and also leads a youth education non-profit organisation.For him, the exercise was an extension of what students learn beyond the classroom.“Ganesh Visarjan is a moment of great faith and celebration, but it also leaves our beaches carrying the weight of that celebration the very next morning,” he says. “This drive is about taking responsibility for that impact; not as an afterthought, but as an extension of what we teach our students, both in the classroom and outside it.”With 207 kilograms of waste removed from the shoreline, Dhabaria says every small action matters. “Every kilogram of waste we pulled off this beach today is a small but real act of care for Mumbai's coastline.”‘ENVIRONMENTAL RESPONSIBILITY FELT REAL’For the students, the exercise offered a lesson that went well beyond textbooks and lectures. Second-year BBA in International Business student Simran Kaur, a Khar resident, says seeing the extent of the waste first-hand changed the way she viewed environmental responsibility.“It was overwhelming to see how much waste had accumulated on the beach in just one night after the immersions,” she says. “Being part of the clean-up made the idea of environmental responsibility feel real and immediate, rather than something we just read about. It's a small effort, but it reminds us that we all have a part to play in keeping our city's coastline clean.”For first-year International Business and Finance student Abhinandan Agrawal, the experience offered a different perspective on a festival he had always associated with celebration. “This was my first time volunteering for a beach clean-up, and it completely changed how I look at Visarjan celebrations,” says the Vile Parle resident. “Seeing idol remains and plastic waste up close made the environmental cost very real for me. ”‘THE CITY FEELS A LITTLE MORE LIKE HOME’For two students who moved to Mumbai from outside the city, the morning carried an added significance. Bhopal resident Juhi Shahani and Piyush Agrawal from Nepal, both pursuing BBA in International Business in Mumbai, had never experienced Ganesh Visarjan up close before moving to the city for college.“Being from out of town, we hadn't seen a Ganesh Visarjan up close before moving to Mumbai for college,” they say. “Waking up early to clean the same beach we'd celebrated on the night before really stayed with us — it made the city feel a little more like home, and reminded us that we're responsible for it too, not just visitors passing through.”MORE THAN A SYMBOLIC GESTUREThe early start was itself a reflection of the commitment behind the exercise. Volunteers were on the ground at 6 a.m., working together to clear the shoreline rather than simply marking the occasion with a symbolic gesture. Vishal Gupta, coordinator with one of the partner organisations, says the effort demonstrated that commitment. “Seeing the entire team come together at 6 a.m. on a Sunday says a lot about the intent behind this drive — it wasn't just symbolic, it was real work. ”By the time the clean-up was over, 207 kilograms of post-Visarjan waste had been removed from the beach. But perhaps the more lasting takeaway was less tangible: for the students who spent their Sunday morning picking up what the celebrations had left behind, the shoreline became a classroom — one that offered a simple lesson in celebrating with faith while taking responsibility for what comes after.
Article Summary: Ganesh Visarjan festivities left behind debris on Juhu Beach, Koliwada, Santacruz. 36 student volunteers collected 207 kilograms of waste, much of it linked to the previous day's immersions. The clean-up was jointly conducted by students from a city college in association with local NGOs.

Article Title: Jewellery store heist in Navi Mumbai: One held, 3 others at large
Article Text:
The CCTV camera footage at the jewellery store has captured two thieves entering the jewellery store after making a huge hole in the common wall and decamping with silver articles on display. However, their attempt to break open the treasury safe in the vault room failed as the alarm siren rang and the thieves fled.





Navi Mumbai: In a breakthrough in the heist at Meghana Jewellers store in Kopri village, sector 26A, Vashi, wherein two men had broken through the common wall of the rented shop and the adjacent jewellery store with tools on Friday around 3 am and had decamped with around 2.5 kg of silver articles estimated to be worth around Rs 6 lakh kept on display at the jewellery store, APMC police arrested one accused from Mankhurd on Sunday.The CCTV camera footage at the jewellery store has captured two thieves entering the jewellery store after making a huge hole in the common wall and decamping with silver articles on display. However, their attempt to break open the treasury safe in the vault room failed as the alarm siren rang and the thieves fled.Abasaheb Patil, senior inspector of APMC, said, “The arrested accused’s identity cannot be revealed, as of now, as it will loosen the strings of the investigation and the three wanted accused will become alert. The arrested accused man was involved in the heist for keeping a watch outside the jewellery store, while the two gang members were breaking the common wall of the rented shop. Four thieves, all hailing from Jharkhand, had executed the crime, including the tenant, who had rented the shop next to the jewellery store, under the guise of fruit selling business. The accused tenant and his two other aides have been identified after the arrested accused disclosed their identity during interrogation. Accordingly, a manhunt has been launched for the other three accused. We have got vital leads of the absconding accused and a police team is tracking them. Only after the three absconding accused are arrested, the stolen silver articles will be recovered.”
Article Summary: Two men had broken through the common wall of the rented shop and the adjacent jewellery store with tools on Friday around 3 am. APMC police arrested one accused from Mankhurd on Sunday. Four thieves, all hailing from Jharkhand, had executed the crime, including the tenant, who had rented the shop under guise of fruit selling business.

Article Title: ​​​Sambhajinagar gears up to bid adieu to Bappa; Greens fume over trees pruning for procession
Article Text:
Trees mercilessly pruned to make way for processions in Sutgirani chowk area

Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar

:

TOI

TOI





Ganapati mandals and households have started preparing for immersion day, marking the conclusion of the Ganeshotsav on Friday.A day before immersion, the atmosphere in the city turned enigmatic, with people feeling emotional but electric. At Ganesh mandals across the city, devotees gathered for the final darshan of Bappa as evening aartis stretched late into the night, and chants of ‘Ganapati Bappa Morya’ echoed louder and distribution of prasad reached its peak.“There was always a bittersweet mood the day before the farewell to Bappa. Like every year, the festival passed so quickly this time too amid the spirit of devotion and spirit,” said Abhishek Ranjangaokar, a youth volunteer with a Ganesh mandal.The city police have also prepared for the immersion day and announced traffic diversions on major procession routes.Environmentalists, however, were outraged after roadside trees from Garkheda Sutgirni Chowk to Jawahar Nagar Police Station have been pruned to clear the route for Ganesh immersion processions.“Branches were pruned cruelly so that 20- to 50-foot-tall idols carried on trucks and tractors face no obstruction,” Dr Kishor Pathak, an environmentalist, told. He alleged that the cutting was done on the instructions of public representatives.Pathak said Ganesh mandals were also disrespecting Lord Ganapati and inviting nature’s wrath by destroying nature.“The civic officials said that trees were being cut against their wishes due to political pressure. The private contractors cut branches in an unscientific manner despite municipal staff being present. If idols of normal height were used, there would be no obstruction of trees,” Pathak said.tried contacting Vijay Patil, garden superintendent of the civic body. He, however, could not be reached for comments by the time of going to the press.

Article Title: LPG leak triggers blast at Sanpada snacks shop in Navi Mumbai, 2 injured
Article Text:
A LPG cylinder leakage caused a blast at a Sanpada snacks shop on Tuesday morning.





NAVI MUMBAI: Two men sustained severe burn injuries after a LPG cylinder leakage triggered a blast at a snacks shop on the ground floor of a society in sector-1, Sanpada on Tuesday morning. The impact of the blast was so severe that the glass facade of a hospital, located about 50 feet away, was shattered. Fortunately, the patients and staff at the hospital were not hurt.Purushottam Jadhav, Divisional officer of Vashi fire station said, "At 6.13 am, the Vashi fire station received the emergency call informing about a cylinder blast at a snacks shop in Pratik CHS on sector-1, Sanpada. The fire bridge team reached the spot within 5 minutes.It was found that the blast was due to leakage in one of the three LPG cylinders kept at snacks shop. The two men working at the snacks shop sustained severe burn injuries and were rushed to NMMC hospital, Vashi. Those injured were identified as Arjun Yadav (46) who has sustained 75 precent burn injuries and Manish Yadav (26), who has sustained 90 percent burns.The blast even caused damage to two shops adjacent to the snacks shop and three other shops in the neighbouring Abhimanyu CHS. While, the glass facade of Suraj hospital located opposite to Pratik CHS was shattered due to the impact of the blast."
Article Summary: Two men sustained severe burn injuries after a LPG cylinder leakage triggered a blast at a snacks shop on the ground floor of a society in Sanpada. The impact of the blast was so severe that the glass facade of a hospital, located about 50 feet away, was shattered. Fortunately, the patients and staff at the hospital were not hurt.

Article Title: 16 years after construction, KDMC mayor finally moves into civic bungalow
Article Text:
The bungalow was constructed in 2010.





KALYAN: Sixteen years after it was constructed, the Kalyan-Dombivli Municipal Corporation’s (KDMC) new mayoral residence at Adharwadi finally got its first regular occupant, with mayor Harshali Chaudhari-Thavil performing the vastu shanti puja and entering the bungalow on Wednesday.The bungalow was constructed in 2010. However, a dispute over access to the property kept the residence largely unused for years. Several mayors subsequently attempted to resolve the road issue, but the efforts failed as villagers whose land was required for the access road were reportedly unwilling to part with the land.Even after the civic body spent lakhs of rupees on repairs, the bungalow remained unused. Former mayor Vinita Rane had performed a puja at the residence but chose not to stay there.With prolonged neglect, wooden furniture inside the bungalow was damaged and several portions were affected by termites. The civic administration later undertook extensive repairs to make the premises habitable again.After taking charge as mayor in February, Thavil took up the long-pending access issue. As she travels daily from Titwala to Kalyan, she personally held meetings with villagers and discussed their concerns. Following the resolution of the issues, the access road was finally constructed, paving the way for the mayoral residence to be used.After the road was made accessible and the neglected bungalow was completely repaired, Thavil finally entered the Adharwadi residence on Wednesday, bringing an end to the 16-year wait for the civic property to be put to its intended use.
Article Summary: Kalyan-Dombivli Municipal Corporation’s new mayoral residence at Adharwadi finally got its first regular occupant. Mayor Harshali Chaudhari-Thavil performed the vastu shanti puja and entered the bungalow on Wednesday.

Article Title: 11 from Malegaon arrested for stealing cellphones during immersion procession

Devotees lost their cellphones to pickpockets while watching the immersion procession in Pune

Pune





: Eleven men from Malegaon in Nashik district were arrested for allegedly stealing cellphones from devotees during the Ganapati immersion procession on Friday and Saturday in Pune. Shivajinagar police recovered a sedan and 63 cellphones worth Rs 30.57 lakh from them.A team headed by deputy commissioner of police (Zone I) Krushikesh Rawale, senior inspector Girish Dhigavkar and inspector Amar Kalange arrested them from a spot off JM Road.Dhigavkar said, “Some of the arrested have cases of thefts registered against them with the Malegaon, Nashik and other police units. Article Title: Cybercrook dupes woman of Rs8L on word of marriage
Article Text:
Pune:

TOI





A 34-year-old married woman was duped of Rs8.14 lakh by a man she met on social media who promised to marry and take her abroad between Aug 27 and Sept 24.She lodged a complaint with Kalewadi police. Article Title: On World Rivers Day, Pune’s river movement seek a Mula-Mutha reconnect
Article Text:
Student participation has become a significant part of the approach. The foundation’s year-long river curriculum is associated with seven city schools and has reached more than 1,500 students

Pune:





A series of conservation activities and a heritage walk with students and other participants along the Mula-Mutha river system marked Jeevitnadi Living River Foundation’s world rivers day programme on Sunday.“The idea is to help people understand the river as an ecosystem and not simply as a water channel. Once people physically come to the river, they understand what is actually there and what is required, rather than deciding what they want the river to be,” said Shailaja Deshpande, founder-director, Jeevitnadi.The heritage walk at Siddheshwar Ghat traced the origin and age of the river, and how the evolution of the Mula-Mutha has shaped Pune’s growth over time. Parallel walks were held at the Ram-Mula confluence and at Vitthalwadi, where experts and volunteers guided participants through the river’s history, ecology, and the challenges it faces today.Student participation has become a significant part of the approach. The foundation’s year-long river curriculum is associated with seven city schools and has reached more than 1,500 students. Students in Classes VI to VIII attend monthly sessions, including nine indoor sessions and a field visit, with each immersive session lasting two hours.“Students learn through direct observation, scientific evidence and documentation. They look at what existed earlier, what remains and what would actually be required to restore it,” Deshpande said.College students also participate in river walks and conservation projects. “Architecture students have worked on spring boxes and ways of protecting groundwater springs. While many colleges have Green Clubs, some also have River Clubs, members of which participate in conservation efforts,” said Shubha Kulkarni, volunteer with Jeevitnadi. “The programme also brings students face-to-face with the consequences of pollution,” Kulkarni added.The foundation’s Adopt a Stretch initiative has now completed nine years. People adopt geographically defined stretches and work there every week or fortnight, going beyond clean-ups to biodiversity mapping, water-quality monitoring, groundwater-spring restoration and documenting changes to the ecosystem.“We are there on different river banks in Pune every Saturday and Sunday morning, throughout the year. on average, 10 to 15 citizens come on regular days, while special activities can bring 50 to 100 people,” said Deshpande.At Vitthalwadi, the initiative has helped restore a groundwater spring and create a wetland in an urban river stretch.During a recent activity, girls from a nearby slum settlement helped remove idols from the river. “River conservation cannot remain an awareness exercise. The connection has to translate into people spending time at the river, understanding it and taking responsibility for a stretch,” Deshpande said.
Article Summary: Jeevitnadi Living River Foundation’s year-long river curriculum is associated with seven city schools and has reached more than 1,500 students. Students in Classes VI to VIII attend monthly sessions, including nine indoor sessions and a field visit, with each immersive session lasting two hours.

Article Title: Woman hides ₹14L jewellery, stages burglary to stop husband from selling it
Article Text:
Pimpri Chinchwad crime branch recover stolen gold jewellery

Pune:

TOI





A 35-year-old woman planned elaborate steps to ensure her husband didn’t sell her gold jewellery to raise money to buy a new house. But her ploy, which included hiding the jewellery and staging a burglary, was unsuccessful.The alleged burglary happened on Sept 25, when the family was out to participate in visarjan. The police quickly unearthed the ruse after her husband, an ex-serviceman from Dighi, lodged a complaint. They have recovered the jewellery and did not arrest the woman.Senior police inspector Santosh Kasbe of Pimpri Chinchwad crime branch toldthat they sent a team to the complainant’s house after he alleged that on Sept 25, gold jewellery worth Rs 14 lakh was stolen from his house while the family was out for Ganesh immersion in the afternoon.“There was no forced entry into the house. We checked CCTV footage and questioned neighbours, but found no clues,” Kasbe said.He said the complainant told the police that before leaving for the immersion, his wife had locked the house and handed the key to him. “We then zeroed in on the woman. During sustained questioning, she admitted to staging the burglary,” Kasbe said.The woman told the police that her husband was planning to buy a new house and wanted to sell her jewellery after Ganeshotsav to raise money.“Worried she would never see her jewellery again, the woman decided to stop her husband from selling it,” Kasbe said.On Sept 25, when everyone left home with the Ganesh idol, the woman hid her jewellery inside the house and scattered her clothes to make it seem like the room was ransacked. She left the door unlocked and gave her husband the key.“When they returned home, they found the door open and the jewellery missing. The woman’s husband then lodged a complaint,” Kasbe said. “The family can collect the jewellery from Dighi police station,” he said.
Article Summary: The 35-year-old woman planned elaborate steps to ensure her husband didn’t sell her gold jewellery to raise money to buy a new house. The alleged burglary happened on Sept 25, when the family was out to participate in visarjan. Her husband, an ex-serviceman from Dighi, lodged a complaint.
